<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par131 />{{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=42|verse=5}} (?), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=11|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=4|verse=42}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=26|verse=14}}.<ref>But in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=17|verse=6}} we should certainly divide the words differently and read {{GHGheb|text=בִּסְעִפֵי הַפֹּֽרִיָּה}}, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=48|verse=44}} read {{GHGheb|text=אֵלֶּה}} for {{GHGheb|text=אֵלֶ֫יהָ}}, and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=14|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=אַֽחֲרִית הַשִּׂמְחָה}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=19}} {{GHGheb|text=נֶ֫פֶשׁ חַיָּה}} is a late gloss upon {{GHGheb|text=לוֹ}}, and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=41|verse=25}} {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־דַּלְתוֹת הַֽהֵיבָל}} a gloss on {{GHGheb|text=אֲלֵיהֶן}}.</ref>—Cf. finally, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=3|verse=7}}, where the suffix precedes the genitive periphrastically expressed by {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁלּ׳}}, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=9|verse=1}}, where the genitive is expressed by {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}.<ref>Some of the examples given above are textually (or exegetically) doubtful, whilst in the case of others, especially those from the later Books, we cannot help asking whether such a prolepsis of the genitive by means of a suffix (as e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=10|verse=3}}) is not due to the influence of Aramaic, in which it is the customary idiom; cf. Kautzsch’s {{GHGcite|title=Gramm. des Biblisch-Aram.}}, {{GHGpar|81|e}} and § 88.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|131|o}}
Of a different kind are the cases in which the permutative with its proper suffix follows as a kind of correction of the preceding suffix, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=29|verse=23}} ''when he'' (or rather) ''his children see'', &c. (but {{GHGheb|text=יְלָדָיו}} is clearly a gloss); cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=83|verse=12}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=29|verse=3}} read {{GHGheb|text=בַּֽהֲהִלּוֹ}} (infin. Hiph.) or at least its syncopated form {{GHGheb|text=בַּהִלּוֹ}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|131|p}}
5. Cases of apposition in a ''wider sense'' are those in which the nearer definition added to the noun was originally regarded as an ''adverbial accusative''; on its use with the verb and on the relative correctness of speaking of such an accusative in Hebrew, cf. {{GHGpar|118|a}} and m. Owing to the lack of case-endings, indeed, it is in many instances only by analogies elsewhere (especially in Arabic) that we can decide whether the case is one of apposition in the narrower or in the wider sense; in other instances this must remain quite uncertain. However, the following are probably cases of apposition in the wider sense:—

{{GHGmargin-letter|131|q}}
(''a'') Such phrases as {{GHGheb|text=מִשְׁנֶה כֶ֫סֶף|translate=a double amount in money}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=15}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=17|verse=18}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=5}} ''five thousand shekels in brass'', but this might also be taken (as in ''d'') ''shekels'' which were ''brass''; certainly such cases as Jb 15<sup>l0</sup> ''older than thy father in days'', and the expression of the superlative by means of {{GHGheb|text=מְאֹד}} (originally a substantive), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=טוֹב מְאֹד|translate=very good}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=31}} (cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=7|verse=16}} {{GHGheb|text=צַדִּיק הַרְבֵּה|translate=righteous over much}}), and the very frequent {{GHGheb|text=הַרְבֵּה מְאֹד}} prop. ''a much-making exceedingly'', i.e. ''exceedingly great'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=49|hidebook=1}}, also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=23|verse=29}} {{GHGheb|text=פְּצָעִים חִנָּם|translate=wounds without cause}},<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=69|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=חִנָּם}} (like {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ֫קֶר|translate=in a false way, falsely}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=35|verse=19}} and 38:20) is used as an ''adverbial accusative'' with a participle; cf. {{GHGpar|118|q}}.</ref> perhaps also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=34|verse=25}} ({{GHGheb|text=בֶּ֫טַח}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|131|r}}
(''b'') A few examples, in which an epexegetical substantive is added to a substantive with a suffix; thus, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=27}} {{GHGheb|text=מִדַּרְכֵּךְ זִמָּה|translate=of thy conduct in lewdness}} (but it is also possible to explain it (as in ''c'') ''of thy conduct'', which is ''lewdness''); cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=24|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=22|verse=33}} {{GHGheb|text=מָֽעוּזִּי חָ֑יִל|translate=my fortress in strength}}, i.e. my strong fortress (cf., however, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=33}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=3|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=71|verse=7}}. While even in these examples the deviation from the ordinary usage of the language (cf. {{GHGpar|135|n}}) is strange, it is much more so in {{GHGheb|text=חֲבֹֽלָתוֹ חוֹב}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=18|verse=7}}, i.e. according to the context ''his pledge'' for ''a debt''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=2|verse=62}} {{GHGheb|text=כְּתָבָם הַמִּתְיַֽחֲשִׂים}}, i.e. ''their register'', namely of ''those that were reckoned by genealogy'' (but perhaps {{GHGheb|text=הַמִּתְי׳}} is in apposition to the suffix in {{GHGheb|text=כְּתָבָם}}), also the curious combinations (mentioned in {{GHGpar|128|d}}) of {{GHGheb|text=בְּרִיתִי}} with a proper name ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=26|verse=42}}), and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=33|verse=20}} with {{GHGheb|text=הַיּוֹם}}.<ref>But in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=25|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=שָׁלוֹם}} may also be explained, according to ''c'', as really in apposition. Cf. on the whole question Delitzsch, ''Psalmen'', 4th ed., p. 203, note 1.</ref><section end=par131 /><noinclude>
